research_text:
# Research brief

## API and meaning of the finding

`java.security.MessageDigest` provides implementations of message-digest algorithms: it processes bytes and returns a fixed-length digest. An object is acquired through `getInstance`, which takes an **algorithm-name string**, optionally with a provider. The message “found MD5” therefore concerns the algorithm associated with an acquisition, not the input data or the resulting digest bytes. The supplied message alone does not establish the resolved call target or a complete execution trace. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

Oracle API: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html`

## Documented usage and security guidance

- Oracle documents acquiring a digest, supplying data with `update`, and completing it with `digest`; completion resets the object. `digest(byte[])` itself performs a final update before completion. Oracle illustrates acquisition with `SHA-256`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
- Oracle lists `MD5` as an algorithm name; that is **not** a recommendation that it is suitable for every security purpose. RFC 6151 says MD5 is unacceptable where collision resistance is required, such as digital signatures. It distinguishes an error-detection-only checksum from a security use. NIST permits the SHA-2 family for applications requiring secure hashes. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- The `MessageDigest` API documentation does not prescribe one universal remediation for MD5 use. A digest comparison alone does not establish authentication or the purpose of the comparison; that purpose is needed to select applicable guidance.

Primary guidance: `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6151/` and `https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/hash-functions/nist-policy-on-hash-functions`

## Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted and wire values:** MD5 produces 128 bits; SHA-256 produces 256 bits. Changing algorithms changes the digest representation and cannot transparently preserve an existing expected MD5 value. Oracle’s API documentation does not specify a general conversion or migration procedure for stored values or external protocols. An unchanged external contract must be considered separately from an internal cache or identifier. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- **A documented protocol-specific path:** HTTP RFC 9530 describes algorithm-labelled digest fields, preferences, and multiple digests to support endpoints with different capabilities or transitions. This is an HTTP mechanism, **not** a migration mechanism supplied by `MessageDigest` or necessarily applicable to another format. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9530/))  
  Source: `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9530/`
- **Platform support:** Java 8 requires `MD5`, `SHA-1`, and `SHA-256`; Java 14 requires `SHA-1` and `SHA-256`; Java 25 requires `SHA-1`, `SHA-256`, and `SHA-384`. These are version-specific minimum requirements, not a guarantee that every allowed rule algorithm is available on every target provider. An unavailable requested implementation can cause `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html?utm_source=openai))
- Oracle advises using standard algorithm names rather than provider-specific aliases. Java algorithm names are case-insensitive, but provider alias availability can differ. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))

## Exact published CrySL rule

The linked file declares `SPEC java.security.MessageDigest` and declares `algorithm` as a `java.lang.String`. Its acquisition matching and algorithm-constraint clauses are, verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;
```

```text
algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512"};
```

Source: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl`

The file thus names `getInstance` in the scope of `java.security.MessageDigest`, with **one or two arguments**; the first is the declared algorithm string, and the second is `_`. It does not specify a type for that second argument in the displayed clause. The listed condition requires membership in the three displayed strings.

**A merely same-named method on an unrelated API is not identified as the governed API by this rule:** the file declares the `MessageDigest` specification scope. The file itself does not define a particular scanner’s type-resolution or erroneous-match behavior, so it cannot establish whether a specific implementation might nevertheless report such a call.

The detector message lists three additional spellings—`SHA256`, `SHA384`, and `SHA512`—that are **not present in the linked file’s literal constraint**. The source does not explain that discrepancy. The link is to a moving `master` branch; the detector’s bundled revision was not supplied, and the provided rule hash was not independently verified. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))
